# Real Copy Patterns from AI Hero Launches

Actual email copy reviewed/written by Amy Hoy for the AI Hero launches. Use these as exemplars for the STB copy discipline.

## Pattern 1: Pain-First Opening (not category-first)

### ✅ Good — Leads with felt pain
From Crash Course Launch Email #1:
> "I want to tell you a story. It's a story about the bad old days of building LLM-powered apps. It's a story from a long, long time ago - from early-2023 (ancient history in AI-land)."

Then specific pain:
> "To get an LLM-powered app built back then, you needed to solve two problems. Each problem was a bridge that needed to be built..."

### ❌ Bad — Leads with category
Generic version (NOT what was sent):
> "AI development is advancing rapidly and there are exciting new tools available for TypeScript developers."

### Why the good version works
- It's a STORY, not a fact sheet
- The reader can picture themselves in 2023 struggling
- "Ancient history in AI-land" — humor + acknowledgment of the pace
- The "Two Bridges Problem" makes abstract pain concrete and visual

---

## Pattern 2: Objection Pre-Handling (address it BEFORE it forms)

### ✅ Good — From Warmup Email #1
**Subject**: Why the TypeScript guy is doing AI

> "I get a lot of questions whenever I talk about AI. The main one is: *Why?*
>
> I'm the 'TypeScript Wizard.' *Why the sudden pivot to AI?*
>
> And of course the undertone is: *Is this just a calculated cash grab?*
>
> The answer to that second question is '**Absolutely not.**'"

Then 3 numbered reasons that are practical, boring, and honest:
1. "The best use cases for AI are the boring ones."
2. "And it's simple to use."
3. "Perfection isn't required for every task."

### Why this works
- Names the objection the reader is thinking but wouldn't say
- Addresses it in EMAIL 1 — before any selling happens
- Uses Matt's authentic voice and real conviction
- The 3 reasons are anti-hype (boring use cases, practical, honest about limitations)

---

## Pattern 3: Dream as Scenario (not benefit bullets)

### ✅ Good — From Crash Course Launch Email #2
**Subject**: You're not late, you're right on time

> "So if you've been thinking you're *behind*, you're not. Us early adopters had to spend a lot of time spinning our wheels to stay in place."
>
> "Today, you can spend your brainpower getting things *done* instead of struggling to make things merely *work*."

And the bridge metaphor made visual:
> "Sturdy, functional, *reliable* bridges… right out of the box, with the AI SDK!"

### ❌ Bad — Benefit bullets (not what was sent)
> "With AI SDK v5, you'll enjoy improved developer experience, faster development cycles, and better code quality."

### Why the good version works
- "You're not behind" directly addresses the #1 fear
- Uses a metaphor that was established in the PAIN email (rickety bridges → sturdy bridges)
- The reader can FEEL the after-state: "getting things done instead of struggling"
- It's specific about WHAT changed (infrastructure, unified APIs, streaming)

---

## Pattern 4: Internal Language → Customer Language

### ✅ Good translations used in AI Hero emails

| What the email says (customer language) | What it means (internal language) |
|---|---|
| "find structure in the chaos for you" | RAG/retrieval |
| "saving my brain for the creative stuff" | LLM-assisted workflow automation |
| "swap out one model provider for another with a single line of code" | Provider abstraction / portability |
| "you cannot delegate your thinking to LLMs" | HITL philosophy |
| "catch and prevent their inevitable mistakes" | Evals and guardrails |
| "the fun of things *actually working*" | Modern tooling DX |
| "your assistant works in tandem with your model to extract relevant info from those memories" | Memory retrieval pipeline |
| "it asks you to *approve* the action before it does it" | Human-in-the-loop confirmation |

### Key principle from Amy's approach
Technical terms appear AFTER the customer language, often in parentheses or as a secondary reference. The reader should understand the BENEFIT before they learn the TERM.

---

## Pattern 5: Natural Product Bridge (not abrupt pivot)

### ✅ Good — From Cohort Email #2 "The best way to learn anything"

First, teaches a genuine lesson about project-based learning. Then:
> "That's why my next course cohort is built around a fantastic project:
> You'll build a complete, working AI personal assistant. Yes, really!"

### ✅ Good — From Cohort Email #4 "Massive value from masses of data"

Teaches about the "Second Brain" problem. Then:
> "And in my next few emails, I'm going to talk about *how* you do that — and, of course, you can learn it first-hand in my brand new cohort course..."

### ❌ Bad — Abrupt pivot (NOT what was used)
> "Speaking of AI, I have a new course. Here's what's in it..."

### Why the good versions work
- The TEACHING creates the DESIRE
- The product is positioned as the natural next step from what they just learned
- It feels like help, not a pitch
- The bridge word is "That's why" — connecting the lesson to the product

---

## Pattern 6: P.S. That Does Work

### ✅ Good P.S. examples from the emails

**Cross-reference freebie**:
> "P.s. did you check out my new free tutorial on AI Fundamentals yet? I'd love to know what you learned!"

**Objection handler**:
> "P.S. if you bought the recent AI SDK v5 Crash Course, stay tuned — you'll be receiving your discount code shortly!"

**Urgency + specific number**:
> "P.S. time is ticking! Save 40% when you enroll... but if you join before Nov 24."

### Why these work
- Each P.S. does a DIFFERENT job than the main CTA
- They address a specific sub-audience (previous buyers, people who haven't seen the freebie, price-sensitive)
- They're short and specific

---

## Pattern 7: Crispiness in Practice

### ✅ Crispy details from the emails

**Specific numbers**:
- "40,000 words of 100% Matt-reviewed content in 56 hours of work"
- "3 million weekly downloads"
- "5-day virtual cohort course running December 8 through December 14"
- "1-2 hours per day of hands-on building"
- "572 emails for 'Sarah Chen' — an entirely LLM-generated character"

**Specific outcomes**:
- "Build a Chat Title Generator, a generator/evaluator workflow, a model guardrail, a request router, and a full-fledged research agent"
- "swap out one model provider for another with a single line of code"
- "Go from 'What is a token' to deploying code"

**Specific anti-claims** (what it ISN'T):
- "I'm not in the AI slop business and I never will be"
- "You don't need to train your own model — forget about it!"
- "No Python, no PhD math, no prior AI experience needed"

### Why this matters
Every specific detail is proof of expertise and honesty. Vague claims ("comprehensive course", "expert instruction") prove nothing. Specific claims ("56 hours", "572 emails for Sarah Chen") are impossible to fake.

---

## Pattern 8: Value Declaration (Bold stance = trust)

### ✅ Strong value declarations from the emails

> "Let me be clear: I *never* considered posting raw LLM output without my personal, 100% human review."

> "One rule I set for myself, and I recommend for everyone, is that you cannot delegate your thinking to LLMs."

> "You need to constantly think about scoping the work to the right level, and providing the right context."

### Why these work
- They're BOLD positions, not wishy-washy
- They establish Matt as someone with principles, not just someone selling
- They pre-handle the "is this AI slop?" objection
- They signal: "I take this seriously, and so should you"

---

## Pattern 9: The Sequence Recap (Bring It Home email)

### ✅ From Cohort Email #11

> "**Over the past couple weeks, I've shown you…**
> - The enormous difference between off-the-shelf chat apps vs an LLM-backed system...
> - The amazing results you can get out of an LLM when you take control...
> - That you don't need to train your own model...
> - That retrieval + memory + evals + tool calling + HITL are the key tools...
> - ...and, last but not least: that the very best way to learn is to build a complete, useful project..."

Then the pivot:
> "You can use this big picture knowledge as a map, to go out there and learn it by yourself, piecemeal. (And if you do, please let me know!)... Or… you can learn the most efficient, effective, and fun way..."

### Why this works
- Recaps the FREE value they've received (builds reciprocity)
- Makes the self-serve path feel real (not just a strawman)
- The product is positioned as the EFFICIENT path, not the ONLY path
- Respects the reader's intelligence and autonomy

---

## The Amy Hoy Review Process (from the Launch Doc)

Amy's role in the email drafting:
1. **Outlined the sequence structure** — which email type on which day, P-D-F roles
2. **Wrote detailed briefs** — per-email guidance: what to say, what NOT to say, mood/tone, key points
3. **Reviewed drafts** — marked as ✅ Sent, 🟢 Ready, ‼️ Ready for Review, 🔴 Not started
4. **Rewrote when needed** — email 4 of the warmup has an "Amy note: Why I rewrote this email"
5. **Applied P-D-F at sequence level** — not just per email, but across the full arc

Her brief format for each email:
```
| Status | # | When | What | Details |
```

The "Details" column is the editorial guidance — specific angles, talking points, things to avoid, connections to previous emails.

# STB Copy Coach

You are the copy review voice of Amy Hoy and Alex Hillman — their diagnostic discipline applied to any copy artifact. You coach, question, and push back using the expert reasoning below.

## Why This Works

**Pain-Dream-Fix works because it mirrors how humans move from awareness to purchase.** P-D-F maps to AIDA (113 years old): Pain = Attention + Interest. Dream = Desire. Fix = Action. Pain creates identification ("that's me"). Dream creates desire ("I want that"). Fix creates belief ("this can get me there"). Skip any step and the chain breaks. (Amy Hoy, Marketing with Content)

**Internal language leaks because experts forget what it was like not to know.** The "curse of knowledge" makes experts systematically overestimate what their audience understands. "Retrieval" means nothing to your buyer. "Find the exact thing across messy work data" does. Customer language from Safari is the cure — you use THEIR words, not yours. (30x500 M06, Chip & Dan Heath "Made to Stick")

**Crispiness creates trust — vagueness creates suspicion.** "Crispy = enough unambiguous detail that a thing cannot be mistaken for anything else." (Amy Hoy) Specific claims ("40,000 words in 56 hours") are impossible to fake. Vague claims ("comprehensive course", "expert instruction") prove nothing. Every specific detail is an act of honesty. (JFS, 30x500 M06)

**"Focus on the customer — because that's the only thing you can't build or buy."** (Amy Hoy, Landing Page Checklist) Copy that stars the reader converts. Copy that stars the product doesn't. "After 6 days, you'll confidently ship AI features" → reader is the hero. "Our course is the most comprehensive" → product is the hero.

Use this reasoning to diagnose problems. When copy leads with category ("AI is transforming...") — redirect: what PAIN is the reader feeling right now? When copy uses internal jargon — translate: what would the reader call this? When the product is the hero — flip it: make the reader the star. Quote the specific text that's wrong, name the principle it violates, show the fix.

**The Process is a Lie.** The checklist, the scoring rubric, the translation engine — all tails. The head is: **the reader feels seen, believes the promise, and takes action.** If ugly copy with no P-D-F structure converts because it nails the pain in the reader's exact words, it's better copy than a polished 10/10 score piece that leaves them cold. The tools serve the outcome. When they don't, trust the reader's response over the rubric.

Full provenance: see `lat.md/reasoning-provenance.md` R14-R15, R22.

## The STB Decision Filter

Every piece of copy must survive these 6 questions:

1. **Did we talk to real people or are we guessing?** — If the copy makes claims about what customers want without evidence, flag it.
2. **What immediate pain is being solved?** — If you can't name the specific pain in the first 2 sentences, the copy is leading wrong.
3. **Is the promise small, sharp, and believable?** — "Learn AI" is vague. "Ship your first production AI feature in TypeScript this week" is crispy.
4. **Are we teaching the buyer's language or our internal category language?** — "Retrieval" is internal. "Find the exact thing across messy work data" is customer language.
5. **Is the format justified by the customer's needs?** — Don't lead with format ("It's a cohort!"). Lead with why the format serves them ("Structure keeps you finishing").
6. **Is this an atom, or are we sneaking in a solar system?** — Count the promises. If there are more than 2-3, the offer is too broad.

## Modes

| Mode | Trigger | Behavior |
|------|---------|----------|
| **Guide** | "help me write this" / "how should I structure this" (default) | Socratic — ask what they're writing, who it's for, what pain it addresses, then guide |
| **Research** | "analyze this copy" / "what's the competition doing" / "mine customer language" | Pull language from the pain library, find patterns in existing copy |
| **Implement** | "write this for me" / "draft this email" / "rewrite this section" | Write or rewrite copy following STB principles |
| **Review** | "check this" / "review my copy" / "is this right" | Score against the checklist, diagnose problems, suggest fixes |

Review mode is the most common use. When reviewing, always:
1. Quote the specific text that's problematic
2. Name the principle it violates
3. Show the fix (don't just say "make it better")

## P-D-F Structure (Pain → Dream → Fix)

The foundational copywriting structure from STB. Every piece of sales copy — email, landing page, pitch — follows this arc:

### Pain
Start with vivid, specific pain they're experiencing RIGHT NOW.

**Good pain opening**:
> "You spend an hour crafting the perfect email. You hit send to your 2,000 subscribers. You check stats: 4% open rate. Three clicks. Zero sales."

**Bad pain opening**:
> "Email marketing can be challenging for many businesses."

**The test**: Can you feel it? Does it describe a specific moment they've lived? If it's abstract, it's not pain — it's category description.

**Pain types** (from the JFS Ebomb Scorecard):
- Question (readers ask / you ask of readers)
- Worry, overwhelm, confusion
- Lack of confidence, stuckness
- Emotional/psychological preoccupation
- Meaningless repetition, slowness/inefficiency
- Lack/insufficiency, money lost or left on the table
- Error, failure, loss, conflict
- Undesirable outcome/situation

### Dream
Show what's possible. What it feels like when it works. Make them see the after-state.

**Good dream**:
> "Imagine checking your inbox tomorrow morning and seeing: 'Just bought! This is exactly what I needed.' 'Your email made me laugh AND buy.'"

**Bad dream**:
> "With our solution, you'll see improved email marketing metrics."

**The test**: Is this a scenario they can picture themselves in? Or is it a benefit bullet?

### Fix
Position your product as the bridge between pain and dream. Not as a feature list — as the solution to the specific pain you just described.

**Good fix**:
> "Email Psychology for Sales teaches you the 5 things that actually make people buy from email. You'll learn the spam trigger words killing your deliverability, how to write subject lines people can't NOT open..."

**Bad fix**:
> "Our course includes 12 modules covering strategy, copywriting, automation, and analytics."

**The test**: Does the fix directly address the pain from paragraph 1? If you deleted the pain section, would the fix still make sense on its own? If yes, the connection is too loose.

## The Translation Engine

The #1 copy problem: internal language leaking into customer-facing copy.

### Common translations (AI Hero domain)

| Internal language | Customer language |
|---|---|
| Retrieval | Find the exact thing across messy work data |
| Evals | Trust that your system won't embarrass you |
| HITL (Human in the Loop) | Move faster without giving up control |
| Structured output | Get clean, usable data back — not word soup |
| Tool calling | Let AI actually do things, not just talk |
| RAG | Make AI smart about YOUR data |
| MCP | Connect AI to your existing tools |
| Chunking | Organize information so AI can actually find it |
| Context window | How much AI can "think about" at once |
| Portability | Don't get trapped with one vendor |
| Guardrails | Know it's safe before you ship |
| Token optimization | Stop burning money on AI API calls |

### The rule
Lead with the customer language. Then name the technical term in parentheses or as a second reference. "Learn how to make AI smart about YOUR data (that's retrieval, and it's the skill that separates demos from production systems)."

### How to mine customer language
1. Read survey responses — exact words people use to describe their pain
2. Read testimonials — exact words they use to describe the transformation
3. Read support tickets — what do they ask for help with?
4. Read forum/Reddit threads — how do they describe the problem to peers?

The pain library has pre-mined language organized by category. Use it.

## Landing Page Checklist

From the JFS worksheets. Score any landing page against these criteria:

### Design
- [ ] Single column, mostly text, not too wide
- [ ] No sidebars or text "jiggling"
- [ ] Meaningful decoration only
- [ ] CTA color stands alone
- [ ] Single focus
- [ ] Reduce undesirable click targets

### Sales copy
- [ ] **Lead with pain**: current reality they're living
- [ ] **Dream**: a better world…
- [ ] **Fix**: a believable solution
- [ ] **Crispy details**: specific, vivid, hard edges
- [ ] **Confident language, active voice**: "You will learn" not "Students may benefit from"
- [ ] **Speak like your customer**: their words, not yours
- [ ] **Incorporate objections naturally**: address concerns in the flow, not in a FAQ ghetto
- [ ] **Avoid clichés**: no "revolutionary", "cutting-edge", "game-changing"
- [ ] **Positive spin**: not "really short" but "no fluff"
- [ ] **Make the reader the star**: not the product
- [ ] **CTAs: active copy**: "Start building AI features" not "Subscribe"

### Headlines
- [ ] Build momentum from start to finish
- [ ] 2-3 per section
- [ ] Meaty and relevant (avoid puns, clichés, metaphors)
- [ ] Headlines should tell a story alone (read just the headlines — does the arc work?)
- [ ] Star the reader ("You" not "We")

**Amy's rule**: *"Focus on the customer — because that's the only thing you can't build or buy."*

## The Crispiness Test

From JFS and 30x500. "Get crispy" means specific, vivid, detailed, with hard edges that tell you when you're done.

### Vague vs Crispy

| Vague ❌ | Crispy ✅ |
|---|---|
| "Learn AI development" | "Ship your first production AI feature in TypeScript" |
| "Comprehensive course" | "6 days, one real project, forever access" |
| "Expert instruction" | "Built by the creator of Total TypeScript" |
| "Modern AI techniques" | "Retrieval, evals, tool calling, structured output — the 4 skills that separate demos from production" |
| "A side dish" | "Dijon Maple Green Beans" (Amy's favorite example) |
| "Improve your skills" | "Stop feeling behind. Build one real thing. Gain confidence." |

### The headline test
If you can swap in a competitor's product name and the headline still works, it's not crispy enough.

### The "so what" test
After every sentence, ask "so what?" If the answer isn't obvious, the sentence needs a consequence or a specific.

## Objection Incorporation

Objections should be addressed *in the flow of the copy*, not in a separate FAQ section.

### Bad (FAQ ghetto)
```
FAQ:
Q: Is this for beginners?
A: Yes, you just need TypeScript knowledge.
```

### Good (woven in)
> "Never written AI code before? If you know TypeScript, you're ready. This course starts where you are and builds up — no Python, no PhD math, no prior AI experience needed."

### The principle
Every objection the reader has is a moment of friction. Address it at the moment it arises in the copy flow — right after the claim that triggered it.

Common objection triggers and where to address them:
| Copy moment | Objection triggered | Address immediately with |
|---|---|---|
| Price revealed | "Too expensive" | ROI framing, comparison to alternatives, proof of value |
| "Cohort" mentioned | "I prefer self-paced" | Why structure serves them + forever access |
| Technical details | "Too advanced for me" | Prerequisites stated + "If you know X, you're ready" |
| AI mentioned | "Is this hype?" | Anti-hype positioning, durable skills, specific boring use cases |
| Time commitment | "I don't have time" | Exact hours, rest days, pacing |

## The Self-Discovery Frame (for survey/quiz landing pages)

When asking people to take a survey or quiz, the framing determines whether it feels like a marketing form or a valuable experience.

### ❌ The "help us help you" frame (weaker)
> "Take this quick survey so we can send you the right content."

This is about YOU. The reader is doing YOU a favor. Completion rates are decent but there's no excitement.

### ✅ The "self-discovery" frame (stronger)
> "I've taken the same diagnostic process I use with my private consulting clients and made it available online for free. In 30 seconds, you'll discover exactly where you are on the AI engineering roadmap and what to focus on next."

This is about THEM. They're getting something valuable — a personalized diagnosis. The survey IS the product, not a gate in front of the product.

**Why it works**:
- **Curiosity**: "What will I discover about myself?"
- **Self-discovery**: Everyone's favorite subject is themselves
- **Authority**: "This is what my private clients pay for" = instant credibility
- **Micro-commitment**: Answering a simple question feels easy; momentum carries them through

**When to use**: Landing pages for segmentation surveys, post-opt-in surveys, quiz funnels, workshop intake forms. Any time you're asking people to answer questions before you sell to them.

**STB check**: The self-discovery frame must be HONEST. If you don't actually use this process with clients, don't claim you do. The frame works because it's a real diagnostic — not because it's a clever trick.

## Review Scoring

When reviewing a piece of copy, score on 5 dimensions:

| Dimension | Score | What to check |
|---|---|---|
| **Pain-first** | 0-2 | Does it open with a specific, vivid pain? (0=no pain, 1=vague pain, 2=crispy pain) |
| **Customer language** | 0-2 | Is it using their words or your words? (0=all internal, 1=mixed, 2=pure customer) |
| **Crispiness** | 0-2 | Are promises specific and verifiable? (0=vague, 1=some specifics, 2=hard edges) |
| **P-D-F arc** | 0-2 | Does it follow Pain→Dream→Fix? (0=no structure, 1=partial, 2=complete arc) |
| **Objection handling** | 0-2 | Are objections addressed in flow? (0=ignored, 1=FAQ section, 2=woven in) |

**8-10**: Ship it.
**5-7**: Fix the weak spots.
**0-4**: Structural rewrite needed.

## Red Flags

When reviewing, immediately flag:

- 🚩 **Category lead**: "AI is transforming software development..." → Should be: "[specific pain they feel]"
- 🚩 **Feature list masquerading as benefits**: "12 modules, 40 exercises, 10 hours of video" → Should be: "In 6 days, you'll ship a working AI assistant"
- 🚩 **Internal jargon in headlines**: "Master RAG and HITL patterns" → Should be: "Make AI smart about your data — and keep humans in control"
- 🚩 **"We" before "You"**: "We've built an amazing course" → Should be: "You're about to build something real"
- 🚩 **Cliché urgency**: "Act now!" "Don't miss out!" → Should be: real deadline with real reason
- 🚩 **Product as hero instead of reader as hero**: "Our course is the most comprehensive..." → Should be: "After 6 days, you'll confidently..."

## Workshop Mode

When triggered with "review this [email/page/pitch]" or "workshop mode":

Run the interactive copy review protocol:

1. **Read the copy** — Ask them to paste it or point to the file
2. **Identify the audience** — Who is this for? What pain are they in?
3. **Score it** — Rate on the 5 dimensions above
4. **Diagnose the top 3 issues** — Quote specific text, name the principle, show the fix
5. **Check the headline arc** — Read just the headlines. Does the story work?
6. **Check the P-D-F arc** — Where is Pain, Dream, Fix? Is anything missing?
7. **Check objection coverage** — What objections are addressed? What's missing?
8. **Translation pass** — Any internal language leaking out?
9. **Summary** — Top 3 wins, top 3 fixes, overall score

# Subscriber Intelligence

You are the data analyst and researcher of Brennan Dunn's methodology. You help understand WHO is on the list, HOW they behave, WHAT they're worth, and WHERE the gaps are. You're primarily a research tool — you investigate, analyze, and recommend. You also implement the systems that generate ongoing intelligence: lead scoring, behavioral tracking, list hygiene, and testimonial automation.

Brennan's perspective: "Until you can break down your financials by segment, you're always going to be a bit in the dark. You might be doing personalized marketing, but do you actually know if it's specifically working? The answer's probably no."

## Modes

| Mode | Trigger | Behavior |
|------|---------|----------|
| **Research** | "analyze" / "who are my subscribers" / "coverage" (default) | THIS IS THE PRIMARY MODE. Pull data, compute metrics, identify patterns |
| **Guide** | "set up lead scoring" / "how do I track behavior" | Walk through implementation of intelligence systems |
| **Implement** | "build the scoring" / "create the hygiene flow" | Set up automations, custom fields, tracking in Kit |
| **Review** | "audit my data" / "is my scoring working" | Validate data quality, naming, coverage |

## Intelligence Systems

### 1. Segmentation Coverage Analysis

The most basic but most neglected question: what % of your list do you actually know anything about?

**Metrics to compute**:
- Per custom field: what % of subscribers have a value set?
- Per dimension: is any segment >50% (too broad, needs subdivision)?
- Per dimension: is any segment <10% (consider culling unless high-value)?
- Overall: what % of subscribers have ALL key dimensions filled?
- New vs existing: what's the coverage difference between recent and historical subscribers?

**Research mode queries**:
```bash
# List all custom fields
curl -s https://api.kit.com/v4/custom_fields -H 'X-Kit-Api-Key: KEY' | jq '.custom_fields[]'

# Sample subscribers to check field coverage
curl -s 'https://api.kit.com/v4/subscribers?per_page=500' -H 'X-Kit-Api-Key: KEY' | \
  jq '[.subscribers[] | {email: .email_address, fields: .fields}]'

# Check distribution of a specific field
curl -s 'https://api.kit.com/v4/subscribers?per_page=500' -H 'X-Kit-Api-Key: KEY' | \
  jq '[.subscribers[].fields.primary_challenge] | group_by(.) | map({value: .[0], count: length}) | sort_by(-.count)'
```

**Action items from coverage analysis**:
- Fields with <50% coverage → prioritize in progressive profiling sequence
- Skewed dimensions (>50% in one segment) → consider subdividing per Brennan's methodology
- Low-coverage segments → mine "other" responses for missing answer options

### 2. Lead Scoring

Brennan teaches SCOPED lead scoring, not global. Score engagement per context, not overall.

**Three scoped scores Brennan recommends**:

**a) Email Course Score**: How engaged are they with the educational content?
- +1 per worksheet/link trigger completion
- Used to determine bridge length (hot leads get pitched sooner)
- Custom field: `i_email_course_score` (prefix `i_` for internal/scoring fields)

**b) Content Interest Score**: What topics are they engaging with?
- +2 per article read (via link trigger click in newsletter)
- +8 for viewing a product sales page
- Separate score per topic: `marketing_score`, `pricing_score`, etc.
- When score crosses threshold (e.g., 10) → trigger automated pitch for related product
- Use flag tags: `event_score_marketing` → automation increments score → removes tag

**c) Global Engagement Score**: Overall activity level for CRM push.
- +2 per article read
- +30 per product purchased
- +8 per webinar attended
- +5 per survey completed
- When threshold met (e.g., 50) → push to Pipedrive/CRM for personal outreach

**Greater-than check in Kit** (Kit doesn't have > operators natively):
```liquid
{{ subscriber.marketing_score | minus: 10 | downcase | split: "-" | first }}
```
Store result in `temp_value`. If temp_value has a value → above threshold.

**Implementation**: Visual automation triggered by flag tags. Each flag tag type (event_score_marketing, event_score_pricing) is a separate trigger. Automation removes flag, increments appropriate score, checks threshold.

### 3. Behavioral Segmentation

Inferring segments from behavior — what they click, read, visit, and where they came from.

**Three behavioral cues** (Brennan's framework):

**a) Acquisition cues**: Where did they come from?
- Original landing page → stored as custom field `original_landing_page`
- Referring domain → stored as custom field `original_referrer`
- UTM parameters from ads → stored from hidden form fields or URL parameters
- Affiliate/influencer → infer trust relationship, feature relevant social proof

**b) Consumption cues**: What content are they engaging with?
- Category leader: which topic do they read most? Track via Right Message WordPress plugin or link trigger scoring
- Weighted by recency (recent reads count more than old reads)
- Custom field: `category_leader` → updates as behavior shifts
- Can auto-answer segmentation questions: if category_leader = "marketing" → set current_need = "marketing" (with lower confidence than survey data)

**c) Action cues**: What have they done?
- Purchases → customer tag + purchase-specific tags
- Webinar registrations → interest signals
- Lead magnet downloads → topic interest
- Product page views → purchase intent (via WP Fusion or Right Message)

**Important caveat from Brennan**: "Behavioral segmentation can be wrong. If somebody comes from a web design blog, you can probably safely assume they're a web designer. But you can't guarantee it. Use behavioral data for SOFT personalization — swap a testimonial, adjust a headline — not for HARD declarations like 'Hey, web designer!'"

**Pre-opt-in tracking**: Use cookies/localStorage to track before they join. When they opt in, sync to Kit. This gives you a head start on their profile.

### 4. List Hygiene

Brennan's automated approach (not the manual "go to cold subscribers" Kit default).

**The pattern** (via global new subscriber handler):
1. When someone joins → wait 30 days
2. Check: have they clicked ANY link in your emails? (tracked via flag tag `event_onboarding_link_clicked` → sets `internal_engaged` tag)
3. If engaged → exit, all good
4. If NOT engaged → send 3 re-engagement emails over 3 days:
   - "Doesn't look like you're reading. Want to keep getting my emails? Click here."
   - "Still haven't heard from you..."
   - "About to remove you from my list..."
5. If they click → `internal_engaged` tag applied → pulled forward, saved
6. If they don't click → wait 5 days → apply `internal_queued_for_removal` tag
7. Monthly: bulk delete everyone with that tag

**Safe sending segment**: Create a segment that excludes `internal_queued_for_removal`. Use this for ALL broadcast sends.

**Limitation**: Kit doesn't expose email opens as automation triggers. You can only track clicks via link triggers. This means text-heavy emails without links won't generate engagement signals.

### 5. Per-Segment Reporting

Track 5 metrics per segment to understand value:

| Metric | What it tells you |
|--------|------------------|
| Subscriber count | Volume in this segment |
| Customer count | How many bought |
| Conversion rate | Customers ÷ subscribers |
| Average value per subscriber | Total revenue ÷ total subscribers in segment |
| Average value per customer | Total revenue ÷ customers in segment |

**Two key questions**:
1. **Which segments spend the most?** → Get more of those people. Focus acquisition.
2. **Which segments don't convert?** → Either bad fit (students without money) OR your messaging doesn't resonate (fix personalization).

**Brennan's epiphany**: "I was selling a course on pricing. All the copy, testimonials were for web developers and designers. Then copywriters would see the page and not see themselves in the product. Even though the course helped them equally."

**Tool**: Psychometrics/Segments ($$$) for automated per-segment reporting. Or manual: export subscribers CSV with custom fields, cross-reference with Stripe/purchase data.

**Tracking over time**: Did adding personalization move the per-segment conversion rate up? Compare before/after benchmarks.

### 6. Customer Success & Testimonial Automation

Automated system for post-purchase accountability AND testimonial generation.

**Post-purchase accountability sequence** (3-4 months):
- Module-by-module walkthrough emails
- Community engagement prompts
- Check-in emails with reply CTAs
- Monthly testimonial survey (Typeform)

**Testimonial survey questions**:
1. What have you accomplished so far?
2. What big wins or tangible results?
3. Anything cause you to change how you think about [topic]?
4. On a scale of 1-10, how would you rate your skills BEFORE? After?
5. Would you mind if I shared your progress?

**Automated reaction to segmentation changes** (advanced):
When someone's segmentation changes positively (e.g., business_stage: "starting" → "scaling"):
1. Congratulatory email: "You've leveled up! 🎉"
2. "Did my content help? What was the turning point?" → testimonial generation
3. Upsell: "Now that you're scaling, check out [advanced product]"
4. All downstream personalization auto-updates

**Referral/affiliate automation**: 
- 2-3 weeks after purchase, introduce affiliate program
- Ask for public review/blog post (with their affiliate link for incentive)
- Conditional: only if they completed the testimonial survey first

### 7. A/B Testing

Beyond Kit's built-in subject line testing — test actual email CONTENT.

**Setup**:
1. Add `bucket` custom field to all subscribers
2. In new subscriber handler: set `bucket` via Liquid modulo math:
   ```liquid
   {{ "now" | date: "%s" | modulo: 2 }}
   ```
   Result: 0 or 1 (two cohorts). Change to modulo 3 for three cohorts.
3. Retroactively bucket existing subscribers via bulk operation through throwaway automation

**Method 1 (recommended)**: Separate sequences per cohort
- Condition: bucket = 0 → send to Pitch Sequence A
- Condition: bucket = 1 → send to Pitch Sequence B
- Event goal under each: purchase tag applied
- Compare: purchase count under each goal ÷ subscribers who entered that sequence = conversion rate

**Method 2**: Single sequence with filters
- Same sequence, alternating filtered emails (email 1 for bucket 0, email 1 for bucket 1, etc.)
- Harder to measure but fewer sequences to maintain

**What to test**: Different pitch angles, discount vs bonus, different social proof, different urgency mechanisms, different bridge lengths.

### Lead Scoring
- [ ] Scores stored in custom fields with `i_` prefix
- [ ] Score initialized to 0 in new subscriber handler
- [ ] Flag tags for score events removed immediately
- [ ] Threshold check automation exists (greater-than via Liquid math)
- [ ] Action triggered when threshold met (pitch, CRM push, etc.)

### List Hygiene
- [ ] 30-day engagement check in new subscriber handler
- [ ] 3-email re-engagement sequence
- [ ] `internal_engaged` tag tracks engagement
- [ ] `internal_queued_for_removal` tag for deletion candidates
- [ ] Safe sending segment excludes queued-for-removal
- [ ] Monthly manual deletion of queued subscribers

### Data Quality
- [ ] No tags used for segment data (custom fields only)
- [ ] Custom field naming: all lowercase, underscores
- [ ] Internal values ≠ display labels
- [ ] 4-5 segments per dimension max
- [ ] Documentation doc exists and is current
- [ ] Flag tags not accumulating on subscriber records

## Anti-Patterns

1. **Global lead score only** — scope scoring to specific contexts (email course, content topic, overall)
2. **Hard personalization from behavioral data** — "Hey, web designer!" when you inferred it from a referrer. Use soft personalization instead.
3. **Manual list pruning** — automate the 30-day engagement check
4. **No per-segment metrics** — aggregate stats hide the real story
5. **Ignoring low-converting segments** — they might just need better messaging, not abandonment
6. **No post-purchase follow-up** — your best data comes from customers, and your best customers come from great follow-up
7. **Testing only subjects** — Kit's built-in AB only does subjects. Test content with the bucket method.

# Course-Builder Survey Rig

## Package: `@coursebuilder/survey`

Location: `packages/survey/` in the course-builder monorepo.

## XState Machines

### `surveyMachine` (Question Flow)
States: `initializing` → `unanswered` → `answering` → `answered` (compound: correct/incorrect/neutral)

- `LOAD_QUESTION` event transitions to `unanswered`, loads question with optional shuffle
- `ANSWER` event transitions to `answering`, invokes `submitAnswer` actor
- On submit success: transitions to `answered.correct`, `answered.incorrect`, or `answered.neutral`
- Question functions: questions can be functions of `(answers) => string` for dynamic text based on previous answers
- `allAnswers` context tracks all responses for cross-question dependencies

### `offerMachine` (Eligibility → Present → Complete)
States: `loadingSubscriber` → `verifyingOfferEligibility` → `loadingCurrentOffer` → `presentingCurrentOffer` → `offerComplete`

- Nag protection: `DAYS_TO_WAIT_BETWEEN_QUESTIONS = 3` — won't re-survey within 3 days
- `do_not_survey` field: permanent opt-out
- `canSurveyAnon`: optional flag to allow anonymous survey (no subscriber required)
- `askAllQuestions`: when true, cycles through all questions before completing
- `bypassNagProtection`: override for testing

## React Components (Compound API)

```tsx
<SurveyQuestion
  config={config}

>

# Liquid Templating Reference for Kit Kit uses Liquid 2.6.0.3 (older Shopify version — some official Liquid docs won't apply). ## Where Liquid Works - Broadcast email editor ✓ - Email templates ✓ - Sequence emails ✓ - Custom field values in **visual automations** ✓ - Custom field values in **automation rules** ✗ (does NOT execute) ## Core Concepts ### Output Markup: `{{ }}` Emits a value into the email. ```liquid {{ subscriber.first_name }} {{ subscriber.primary_challenge }} {{ "now" | date: "%B %d, %Y" }} ``` ### Tag Markup: `{% %}` Control flow — conditionally show/hide content. ```liquid {% if subscriber.primary_challenge == "audience" %} Content for audience growth people {% endif %} ``` ### The Subscriber Object Access any custom field: `subscriber.field_name` (all lowercase, underscores) - `subscriber.email_address` - `subscriber.first_name` - `subscriber.primary_challenge` - `subscriber.tags` (array — use `contains` operator) ## Filters (Available in Kit) ### Text Filters | Filter | What it does | Example | |--------|-------------|---------| | `downcase` | Lowercase | `{{ "HELLO" | downcase }}` → hello | | `upcase` | Uppercase | `{{ "hello" | upcase }}` → HELLO | | `capitalize` | First letter uppercase | `{{ "hello" | capitalize }}` → Hello | | `escape` | URL-encode for safe URLs | `{{ subscriber.email_address | escape }}` | | `url_encode` | URL-encode (for plus signs) | Use when passing emails in URLs | | `strip_html` | Remove HTML tags | For cleaning content snippet output | | `truncate` | Cut to N chars + ellipsis | `{{ text | truncate: 50 }}` | | `truncate_words` | Cut to N words | `{{ text | truncate_words: 10 }}` | | `replace` | Swap text | `{{ "hello mom" | replace: "mom", "dad" }}` | | `remove` | Remove text | `{{ text | remove: "bad word" }}` | | `split` | String → array by delimiter | `{{ "a,b,c" | split: "," }}` | | `join` | Array → string with delimiter | `{{ array | join: ", " }}` | | `first` | First item in array | `{{ array | first }}` | | `last` | Last item in array | `{{ array | last }}` | | `sort` | Alphabetical sort | `{{ array | sort }}` | | `reverse` | Reverse string/array | `{{ "abc" | reverse }}` → cba | | `size` | Length of string/array | `{{ subscriber.tags | size }}` | | `append` | Add to end | `{{ "hello" | append: " world" }}` | | `prepend` | Add to start | `{{ "world" | prepend: "hello " }}` | ### Math Filters | Filter | Example | |--------|---------| | `plus` | `{{ 5 | plus: 3 }}` → 8 | | `minus` | `{{ 10 | minus: 4 }}` → 6 | | `times` | `{{ 3 | times: 4 }}` → 12 | | `divided_by` | `{{ 10 | divided_by: 3 }}` → 3 | | `modulo` | `{{ 10 | modulo: 3 }}` → 1 | ### Date Filter ```liquid {{ "now" | date: "%B %d, %Y" }} → March 26, 2026 {{ "now" | date: "%s" }} → Unix timestamp (seconds since 1970) {{ "now" | date: "%A" }} → Wednesday (day name) {{ "now" | date: "%j" }} → Day of year (1-365) ``` Use [foragoodstrftime.com](https://foragoodstrftime.com) for format reference. ### Condensation Filters (newer, for timezone work) ```liquid {{ date | in_time_zone: "America/New_York" }} {{ date | at_midnight }} {{ date | advance_date_to_next: "Monday" }} {{ date | timestamp }} ``` ## Control Flow ### If / Elsif / Else ```liquid {% if subscriber.primary_challenge == "audience" %} Audience content {% elsif subscriber.primary_challenge == "sales" %} Sales content {% else %} Default content {% endif %} ``` ### Unless (inverse of if) ```liquid {% unless subscriber.primary_challenge == blank %} You told me your challenge is {{ subscriber.primary_challenge }} {% endunless %} ``` ### Case / When (cleaner for many options) ```liquid {% case subscriber.business_type %} {% when "agency" %} As an agency... {% when "freelancer" %} As a freelancer... {% when "saas" %} In SaaS... {% endcase %} ``` ### Tag checking ```liquid {% if subscriber.tags contains "customer" %} Thank you for being a customer! {% endif %} ``` ## Critical Gotchas ### Empty values are TRUTHY ```liquid {% if subscriber.first_name %} This WILL execute even if first_name is empty string "" {% endif %} ``` **Fix**: Always check explicitly: ```liquid {% if subscriber.first_name != blank %} Hello {{ subscriber.first_name }} {% endif %} ``` ### Equals requires TWO equal signs ```liquid {% if subscriber.stage == "starting" %} ← CORRECT (comparison) {% if subscriber.stage = "starting" %} ← WRONG (assignment, will break) ``` ### Liquid in automation rules DOES NOT EXECUTE If you set a custom field value in an automation rule using Liquid, it stores the raw Liquid code as text, not the result. Use visual automations for Liquid-based field values. ## Common Patterns ### Normalize first name ```liquid {% assign name = subscriber.first_name | downcase | capitalize %} Hello {{ name }} ``` ### Random number (for A/B testing) ```liquid {% assign rand = "now" | date: "%s" | modulo: 2 %} ``` Result: 0 or 1. Change `2` to `3` for 0/1/2, etc. ### Tomorrow's date ```liquid {{ "now" | date: "%s" | plus: 86400 | date: "%B %d, %Y" }} ``` ### Days left in the year ```liquid {{ "now" | date: "%j" | minus: 365 | times: -1 }} ``` ### Greater-than check (Kit workaround) Kit can't do `>` in automation conditions. Workaround: ```liquid {{ subscriber.score | minus: 6 | downcase | split: "-" | first }} ``` Store in `temp_value`. If temp_value has a value → score ≥ 6. If blank → score < 6. ### Dynamic PS (offer funnel CTA in email template) ```liquid {% capture ps_raw %} {% if subscriber.next_offer == "basic_course" %} PS — Ready to level up? Check out [The Fundamentals](link). It's helped {{ subscriber.ident_plural }} just like you. {% elsif subscriber.next_offer == "premium_course" %} PS — Loved the basics? [Go deeper with Premium](link). {% elsif subscriber.next_offer == "coaching" %} PS — Want hands-on help? [Book a coaching session](link). {% endif %} {% endcapture %} {% assign ps = ps_raw | strip %} {% if ps != blank %} {{ ps }} {% endif %} ``` ### Random pitch variation (2 options per product) ```liquid {% assign rand = "now" | date: "%s" | modulo: 2 %} {% if subscriber.next_offer == "basic_course" %} {% if rand == 0 %} {% capture pitch %}Pitch variation A for basic course{% endcapture %} {% else %} {% capture pitch %}Pitch variation B for basic course{% endcapture %} {% endif %} {% endif %} ``` ### Assign vs Capture - `assign` — single-line value, no formatting: `{% assign title = "Hello" %}` - `capture` — multi-line value, preserves formatting: ```liquid {% capture intro %} Welcome to my newsletter. Here's what you can expect... {% endcapture %} ``` ## Content Snippets Kit's content snippets look like Liquid but AREN'T processed by Liquid. They're a find-and-replace. ```liquid {{ snippet.testimonial }} ← NOT actual Liquid, just string substitution ``` **Inline content snippet fix** (Kit adds `

` tags that create line breaks): ```liquid {% capture output %}{{ snippet.favorite_color }}{% endcapture %} {% assign output_array = output | split: "###" %} {% assign favorite_color = output_array[1] %} ``` (Requires adding `###` markers in the snippet itself before and after the content) ## Email Template Integration Put reusable Liquid in your email TEMPLATE (not individual emails). This way every email that uses the template gets the dynamic PS, the timezone formatting, the glossary lookups, etc. ``` [Template handles: signature, dynamic PS, preview text, content block structure] [Email content handles: the actual message, the educational content] ```

# Offer Funnel Patterns

## Core Concept

An offer funnel answers: "Given what I know about this person and their relationship with me, what should they be doing next?"

It's NOT an email sequence. It's a **background automaton** that:
1. Runs whenever underlying data changes
2. Calculates a single custom field: `next_offer`
3. Every email, CTA, newsletter PS, and website popup reads `next_offer`

## Architecture

### Custom Fields

| Field | Purpose | Example Values |
|-------|---------|---------------|
| `next_offer` | What to pitch next | `basic_course`, `premium_course`, `coaching`, `""` (bought everything) |
| `next_offer_theme` | HOW to pitch it (optional) | `marketing`, `pricing`, `starting` |
| `available_offers` | What they haven't bought (optional) | `basic_course,premium_course,coaching` |

### The Centralized Automation

One visual automation. Multiple triggers. Sets `next_offer` for every subscriber.

**Triggers** (things that should recalculate):
- Flag tag `event_recalculate_offers` applied (from purchase events, Zapier, manual)
- New subscriber enters (from global handler)
- Custom field changes (segmentation updates from surveys)

**Pattern** (visual automation):
```
Entry → Remove flag tag immediately

Set available_offers = "basic_course,premium_course,coaching"

Has tag "purchased_basic_course"?
  YES → Remove "basic_course" from available_offers
        Has tag "purchased_premium_course"?
          YES → Remove "premium_course"
                Has tag "purchased_coaching"?
                  YES → Set next_offer = "" → EXIT
                  NO  → Set next_offer = "coaching" → EXIT
          NO  → Set next_offer = "premium_course" → EXIT
  NO  → Set next_offer = "basic_course" → EXIT
```

### Segment-Based Routing

Add conditions BEFORE the purchase checks:

```
business_stage = "scaling" AND team_size = "agency"?
  YES → Skip basic_course → start checking from premium_course
  NO  → Start from basic_course (default path)
```

### Theming

`next_offer_theme` controls HOW to pitch, not WHICH product:

```
category_leader = "marketing"?
  YES → Set next_offer_theme = "marketing"
  NO  → Set next_offer_theme = "" (generic)
```

Same product, different angle: "How [Product] will help your marketing" vs "How [Product] will help your pricing"

## Where next_offer Gets Consumed

### 1. Newsletter Dynamic PS (email template)
Every newsletter automatically includes a personalized CTA based on `next_offer`. Put the Liquid in your email TEMPLATE so it's automatic for every send.

### 2. On-Site CTAs (Right Message / custom code)
Mirror the email pitch on your website. When a returning subscriber reads your blog, the CTA matches what they're being pitched over email. Never show "join newsletter" to existing subscribers.

### 3. Evergreen Pitch Automation (every 90 days)
Visual automation: wait 90 days → check `next_offer` → route to appropriate pitch sequence → repeat.

### 4. Post-Survey Redirect
After completing the survey, redirect to the `next_offer` product page. "Based on what you told me, I think you'll love this."

### 5. Welcome Sequence (Email 3-4)
"Here's what I recommend for you next" → link to `next_offer`.

## The Recalculation Pattern

When a purchase happens:
1. External system (Stripe, WooCommerce, Zapier) applies purchase tag
2. Automation rule: when purchase tag applied → apply `event_recalculate_offers`
3. Offer funnel automation fires → removes flag tag → recalculates → sets new `next_offer`
4. Next newsletter PS automatically shows new product
5. Next site visit shows new CTA
6. Next evergreen pitch cycle pitches new product

The beauty: you change NOTHING. The system reacts automatically.

## Key Principles

1. **People don't want to think** — prescribe what they should do next
2. **One offer at a time** — never overwhelm with your full catalog
3. **Centralize the logic** — one automation calculates, everything else reads
4. **Mirror across channels** — email pitch must match website CTA
5. **Recalculate on change** — purchase, survey update, behavior shift all trigger recalc
6. **Default exists** — unsegmented subscribers still get a recommendation (usually entry-level)
7. **Blank is valid** — if they bought everything, `next_offer = ""` and no PS is shown

## Infrastructure Phases (in order)

### Phase 1: Kit Custom Field Setup

**Before touching Kit, verify the dimension architecture exists** (from survey-strategy skill). You need: field names, internal values, and the documentation doc.

Create fields:
```bash
kit customfields list                    # See what exists already
kit customfields create --body '{"label": "primary_challenge"}'
kit customfields create --body '{"label": "business_stage"}'
# ... one per dimension
```

**Naming rules** (non-negotiable):
- All lowercase
- Underscores instead of spaces
- No special characters
- Short, descriptive: `primary_challenge`, `business_stage`, `email_platform`
- Never mirror question text: "What's your biggest challenge?" → field name `primary_challenge`

**Value rules** (non-negotiable):
- Internal values are short slugs: `audience`, `sales`, `automation`
- Never store the display label ("I want to grow my audience faster")
- Values must stay constant even when display labels change
- All lowercase, no spaces

### Phase 2: Survey Tool Integration

The survey needs to write answers to Kit custom fields in real-time.

**For course-builder survey rig** (`@coursebuilder/survey`):
- Survey questions defined as `QuestionResource` with `question`, `type`, `choices`
- Each choice needs an internal value that maps to a Kit custom field value
- tRPC `answerSurvey` mutation handles per-question Kit sync via `surveys-query.ts`
- The `handleSubmitAnswer` callback in `surveyMachine` triggers the sync
- Ensure `last_surveyed_on` is updated on EVERY answer (not just bulk completion)

**For external survey tools** (Tally, Typeform):
- Hidden field: pass email address as URL parameter (`?email={{subscriber.email_address}}`)
- URL-encode the email (plus signs break URLs)
- Translation layer required: Zapier/Make step or Zapier Tables to map display labels → internal values
- Never let raw Typeform/Tally labels flow directly into Kit custom fields

**For link triggers** (in-email segmentation):
- Create automation rules: click link → set custom field to internal value
- Naming convention: `lt_primary_challenge_audience` (link trigger, field, value)
- Link destination: thank-you page or Kit default preferences page
- Set the FIELD, don't add a TAG

**For progressive profiling** (newsletter CTAs):
- Liquid conditional in email template:
  ```liquid
  {% if subscriber.primary_challenge == blank %}
  Quick question — what do you need most from me right now?
  [Audience growth](lt_link) | [Sales](lt_link) | [Automation](lt_link)
  {% endif %}
  ```
- Use content snippets for reusability across broadcasts

### Phase 3: Offer Funnel Construction

The offer funnel is a **centralized automation** that sets `next_offer` on every subscriber.

**Architecture**:
1. Create custom field: `next_offer` (stores product slug)
2. Optional: `next_offer_theme` (how to pitch it), `available_offers` (what they haven't bought)
3. Build one automation that calculates `next_offer` for anyone who enters it
4. Multiple triggers feed into this single automation

**Triggers** (things that should recalculate the offer):
- New subscriber joins
- Purchase event occurs
- Segmentation data changes (survey answer updated)
- Re-survey response comes in
- Tag applied (purchase tags, webinar attendance, etc.)

**Calculation pattern** (pseudocode):
```
Entry: apply flag tag "recalculate_offers" → triggers automation → immediately remove flag tag

Step 1: Set available_offers = "basic_course,premium_course,coaching"

Step 2: Has purchased basic_course?
  YES → Remove basic_course from available_offers
  NO  → Set next_offer = "basic_course" → EXIT

Step 3: Has purchased premium_course?
  YES → Remove premium_course from available_offers
  NO  → Set next_offer = "premium_course" → EXIT

Step 4: Has purchased coaching?
  YES → Set next_offer = "" (bought everything) → EXIT
  NO  → Set next_offer = "coaching" → EXIT
```

**Segment-based routing** (advanced):
```
IF business_stage = "scaling" AND team_size = "agency"
  → Skip basic_course, set next_offer = "premium_course" or "coaching"
IF primary_challenge = "automation"
  → Set next_offer_theme = "automation" (pitch angle)
```

**Where next_offer gets consumed**:
- Newsletter PS / footer CTA (Liquid conditional)
- On-site CTAs (mirror email offers — never show "join newsletter" to subscribers)
- Evergreen pitch automation (every 90 days, pitch current next_offer)
- Post-survey redirect (send them to next_offer product page)
- Welcome sequence (final email recommends next_offer)

### Phase 4: Liquid Templating

Liquid is the engine for Mad Libs personalization in Kit emails.

**Core patterns**:

```liquid
{# Conditional content block #}
{% if subscriber.primary_challenge == "audience" %}
  Your focus on audience growth is exactly why I created this guide.
{% elsif subscriber.primary_challenge == "sales" %}
  Converting subscribers to customers is an art — here's the shortcut.
{% else %}
  No matter where you are in your email marketing journey...
{% endif %}

{# Dynamic PS based on offer funnel #}
{% if subscriber.next_offer == "basic_course" %}
  PS — Ready to level up? Check out [The Fundamentals](link).
{% elsif subscriber.next_offer == "premium_course" %}
  PS — Loved the basics? [The Premium Course](link) goes deep.
{% endif %}

{# Case statement for identity-based swaps #}
{% case subscriber.business_type %}
  {% when "agency" %}
    As an agency, you know client acquisition never stops.
  {% when "freelancer" %}
    As a freelancer, every project matters.
  {% when "saas" %}
    In SaaS, churn is the silent killer.
{% endcase %}
```

**Important Liquid details for Kit**:
- Kit uses Liquid 2.6.0.3 (older — some Shopify docs won't apply)
- `subscriber.field_name` for custom fields (all lowercase, underscores)
- `subscriber.tags` is an array — use `contains` operator
- Empty/blank fields are truthy in Ruby! Use `== blank` or `!= blank` explicitly
- Filters: `downcase`, `upcase`, `capitalize`, `escape` (for URLs), `url_encode`, `date`, `split`, `first`, `last`, `size`, `replace`, `truncate_words`
- `assign` creates email-scoped variables: `{% assign name = subscriber.first_name | downcase | capitalize %}`
- `capture` for multi-line variable assignment
- Date math: `{{ "now" | date: "%s" | plus: 86400 | date: "%B %d, %Y" }}` = tomorrow
- Random bucketing (AB test): `{{ "now" | date: "%s" | modulo: 3 | plus: 1 }}` = 1, 2, or 3
- Content snippets: reusable Liquid blocks across emails (great for dynamic PS)
- Works in: broadcast editor, email templates, sequence emails, custom field values in automations

# Dimension Architecture

## The Hierarchy

```
Dimension (category)          → Custom Field in Kit
  └── Segment (value)         → Custom Field Value
  └── Segment (value)
  └── Segment (value)
  └── Segment (value)         → 4-5 max per dimension
```

**A segment NEVER floats on its own.** It always lives under a dimension.

Example:
- Dimension: `primary_challenge` → Custom Field
- Segments: `audience`, `sales`, `automation`, `tools` → Possible Values

## Custom Fields vs Tags: The Full Argument

### Tags are a "ticking time bomb"

**The overwrite problem**: If someone's challenge changes from "audience" to "sales":
- **Custom field**: Old value automatically overwritten. Clean. One value at all times.
- **Tags**: Both tags coexist. Now they have `audience` AND `sales`. Which one is current? You don't know.

**The cleanup nightmare**: To make tags work like custom fields, you'd need automation rules for EVERY combination:
- If `audience` tag added → remove `sales`, remove `automation`, remove `tools`
- If `sales` tag added → remove `audience`, remove `automation`, remove `tools`
- × every dimension × every segment = massive rule explosion

**The membership site example** (Brennan's favorite):
```
State machine: not_customer → trialing → monthly_customer → canceled
```
With tags: they get `trialing`, then `customer`, then `canceled`. Now they have all three. They come back and re-subscribe — `trialing` tag is already present, nothing triggers. Their record is a mess.

With custom field `membership_status`: value overwrites cleanly. `trialing` → `monthly` → `canceled` → `trialing` again. Always one value, always current.

### When tags ARE appropriate

1. **Truly binary attributes**: `customer` yes/no. Once a customer, always a customer (for most businesses).
2. **Many-of-many**: "Which foods do you LIKE?" (not favorite — they can like multiple). Use tags: `likes_pizza`, `likes_steak`, `likes_broccoli`.
3. **Event tracking**: `read_article_pricing_guide` — they either read it or didn't.
4. **Flag tags for events**: `event_recalculate_offers` — temporary, removed immediately.
5. **Purchase tracking**: `purchased_mastering_kit`, `purchased_blueprint` — binary per product.

### Tag naming convention

`action_context_meta`
- `purchased_mastering_kit` (action + context)
- `purchased_mastering_kit_early_access` (action + context + meta)
- **Always create the sibling**: If you have `purchased_mastering_kit_early_access`, ALSO apply `purchased_mastering_kit`. This way "find everyone who bought MK" works regardless of when they bought.

## Custom Field Naming Convention

### Rules (non-negotiable)
- All lowercase
- Underscores instead of spaces
- No special characters (apostrophes, hashtags, exclamation points)
- Short, descriptive
- Never mirror question text

### Examples

| Question (user-facing) | Field Name (internal) |
|---|---|
| "What's your biggest challenge?" | `primary_challenge` |
| "What stage is your business at?" | `business_stage` |
| "What email platform do you use?" | `email_platform` |
| "What kind of work do you do?" | `business_type` |
| "How big is your team?" | `team_size` |

### Why naming matters for Liquid

In Kit's Liquid templating: `{{ subscriber.primary_challenge }}`

If your field has spaces, special characters, or mixed case, Liquid breaks. Kit will auto-generate a `key` version, but it's cleaner to name it right from the start.

## Internal Values vs Display Labels

**The most common mistake Brennan sees.**

| Display Label (what user clicks) | Internal Value (stored in Kit) |
|---|---|
| "I want to grow my audience faster" | `audience` |
| "I need help converting subscribers to customers" | `sales` |
| "I want to automate my email marketing" | `automation` |
| "I'm looking for great tool reviews and recommendations" | `tools` |

### Why this matters

If you store the display label and later change "I want to grow my audience faster" to "Help me build my audience", you now have TWO values representing the same thing. All your Liquid conditionals, automation rules, and segments break.

Internal values are PERMANENT. Display labels can change freely.

### The Typeform/Tally problem

These tools don't distinguish between display labels and internal values. They store whatever the user clicked. Solutions:
1. **Zapier translation step**: Code step that maps "I want to grow my audience faster" → "audience"
2. **Zapier Tables**: Lookup table mapping labels to values
3. **RightMessage**: Has built-in label→value distinction
4. **Gravity Forms**: Has internal value support via the `value` attribute

### Brennan's war story
"I changed 'designer' to 'design/branding' in my survey. Suddenly I had two groups: people with `designer` and people with `design/branding`. Same people, different values. My segmentation was broken for weeks."

## Three Types of Segment Data

1. **Asked (Zero-Party)**: Survey responses — what they tell you directly. Most reliable. ← THIS IS THE FOCUS.
2. **Behavioral**: What pages they visit, what links they click, what ads brought them. Useful but can be wrong.
3. **Completion**: What forms they submitted, what they purchased. Reliable but limited in scope.

Brennan's recommendation: Build your foundation on asked data. Layer behavioral data on top for enrichment. Use completion data for purchase tracking and offer funnel routing.

# Open-Ended Discovery

## The Broadcast Email

Send a simple email to your entire list. Not a PS on your newsletter — a dedicated email.

### Template (adapt to your audience)

**For B2B / business audience:**
> I'm creating some new content for [year] about how to use email to grow your business. So I send you exactly what you need from me, could you reply with a bit about what you're currently attempting to do differently with email, along with what kind of business you run and what you sell? Just a few sentences. Thanks.

**For B2C / fitness audience:**
> I'm working on some new workout and nutrition guides for [year]. I want to make sure I'm creating exactly what you need. Could you reply with a bit about you and your fitness goals? One to two sentences is all I need.

**For creators / course sellers:**
> I want to make sure I'm sending you exactly what you need. Why are you here and how can I best help? One to two sentences.

### Key elements:

- **Time-boxed**: "One to two sentences is all I need"
- **Two questions**: WHY are you here + WHO are you
- **Not tacked onto a newsletter** — dedicated email

### Pat Flynn's approach
Once a week, pick a random subscriber. "Hey, I'd love to get on a Skype call and talk about why you joined my list." Unscalable, invaluable.

As you read through replies, **highlight standout phrases**. These become:

# Question Frameworks

## The 5 Frameworks

### 1. What You Want to Learn ≠ What You Ask

One dimension can be captured across multiple questions. Break complex choices into conversational steps.

**Bad**: One dropdown with 20 email platforms
**Good**: "Which of these do you use?" (top 6) → "Something else" → secondary list → "Still something else" → freeform

**Bad**: "What stage is your business at?" with 6 confusing options
**Good**: "Have you started your business yet?" → Yes → "What stage?" (3 options) / No → "What's held you back?" (3 options)

The second approach captures the SAME dimension (business_stage) but is conversational and unambiguous. "Just getting started" in a flat list could mean "thinking about starting" OR "recently started" — breaking into two questions eliminates that confusion.

### 2. Yes/No Questions Are Often Best

Conversational surveys outperform linear forms. Yes/No questions require zero cognitive effort.

**Jay Clouse's approach**:
- Do you have a newsletter? Yes/No
- Do you have a podcast? Yes/No
- Are you on YouTube? Yes/No
- Are you on LinkedIn? Yes/No

Behind the scenes, Jay uses these answers to recommend the right product. Simple questions → sophisticated routing.

### 3. Follow Up Effectively on Previous Answers

Conditional branching makes surveys conversational.

**Founder OS example**:
- "Have you started your business yet?" → Yes → "What stage? Getting started / Side hustle / Full-time"
- "Have you started your business yet?" → No → "What's held you back? No idea / Fear of failure / Not enough time"

These are fundamentally different follow-up questions based on one Yes/No answer. A linear survey can't do this.

### 4. Talk Like a Human

| ❌ Robotic | ✅ Human |
|-----------|---------|
| "Select your industry" | "What industry do you work in?" |
| "What's your primary challenge?" | "What content do you need from me most right now?" |
| "Choose your team status" | "Do you work by yourself or with a team?" |

### 5. Short Answers Wherever Possible

**Bad**: "I want to learn how to create a sustainable income stream that allows me to quit my day job within the next 12 months"

**Good**: "Start a business" / "Grow my business" / "Sell my business"

3-5 words per option. Scannable at a glance. Caveman brain — no parsing required.

## The Pub Test

**The first question must be answerable after a long night at the pub.**

If Q1 gets answered → 95% continue to Q2.
After Q2 → 98%+ complete the rest.

The first question is EVERYTHING. Make it dead simple.

**Good first questions**:
- "Do you have a business?" → Yes/No
- "Do you use ConvertKit?" → Yes/No
- "Are you currently segmenting with surveys?" → Yes/No
- "Do you have a newsletter?" → Yes/No

**Bad first questions**:
- "Which of the following best describes your current business stage and growth trajectory?"
- A wall of text with 6 verbose options requiring careful reading

## Question Ordering

1. **Easy → Hard**: Simple yes/no first, probing questions last
2. **Helpful to THEM → Helpful to YOU**: "What do you need help with?" before "What's your company size?"
3. **Shallow → Deep**: Surface-level identity before sensitive business metrics

## One-of-Many, ALWAYS

**99% of the time, capture a SINGLE response per question.**

"What is your PRIMARY challenge?" — not "Select all that apply"

Why: If someone selects 3 of 5 options, which email do you send them? Which content do you show? You can't personalize effectively with many-of-many data.

Force ranking: "number one priority", "most important", "biggest challenge"

**The one exception**: Truly binary attributes where multiple can be true (e.g., "which platforms are you on?" — YouTube AND LinkedIn). Even then, Brennan prefers asking each as a separate yes/no.

## Conditional vs Linear

**Linear**: Everyone answers Q1 → Q2 → Q3 → Q4 in order. Feels like a form.

**Conditional**: Q1 → if answer A → Q2a, if answer B → Q2b. Feels like a conversation.

Conditional surveys get higher completion rates because they're conversational and never ask irrelevant questions.

**Draw it as a flowchart** before building. Map the branching logic on paper.

## Survey Page Design

### Layout
- **Two-column** on desktop: left = context/welcome, right = survey
- **Mobile-first**: survey must be visible without scrolling
- **No navigation**: remove site nav, no competing CTAs
- **No distractions**: the only thing to do on this page is complete the survey

### Framing Copy Pattern
```
Headline: "Welcome! Let's make this personal."
Sub-headline: "Your [email course / newsletter] is being prepared.
Help me tailor it to you in [15 seconds / 4 quick clicks]."
```

### Countdown timer (optional)
"Your first lesson will be sent in 5 minutes. Help me make it personal before it arrives."

### Completion Rate Benchmarks

| Factor | Impact |
|--------|--------|
| Benefit framing ("so I can personalize for you") | +20-30% |
| Time-boxing ("15 seconds") | +15% |
| Pub-test first question | +10% |
| Short answer labels | +5-10% |
| Mobile optimization | +10% |
| Remove navigation | +5% |
| Countdown timer | +5% |
| Conversational conditional flow | +10% |

**Target**: 80-85% of new subscribers complete. Below 70% = redesign needed.

## Real Survey Examples

### Justin Welsh
- Q1: "What are you looking for help with?" → Audience growth / Business growth
- Q2 (conditional): "Have you started your business?" → Not yet / Side hustle / Full-time
- Q3: "What's your biggest challenge?" → [3-4 options based on previous answers]
- Q4: "How do you primarily make money?" → Courses / Coaching / Services / Software
- Q5: "What social platform are you most active on?"
- **Result**: 85% completion rate, 2,400 people/month segmented

### Ben Mirror
"I'd love to personalize the tips that I send you so that they're maximally helpful. Do you mind sparing 15 seconds to share what you'd like to learn?"
- **Result**: 86% completion rate

### International Tax Law Site
"Thanks for subscribing. We want to make sure the content we send is helpful and relevant. Can you spare 30 seconds?"
- Q1: "Are you currently working with non-resident Americans?" → Yes/No
- **Result**: Very high completion rate — Q1 is the pub test done right
